intro: The figurative expressions you hear in meetings, internal emails and interviews. Understanding them prevents misunderstandings; using them accurately makes your English sound natural and credible.
objectifs: Understand around thirty common workplace idioms (meetings, projects, workload, results).
Use them in their exact form: the right preposition, article and possessive, and the right tense.
Choose the right register: an idiom in a meeting or internal email, a neutral equivalent in formal writing or with a client.
Recognise irritating corporate jargon (circle back, synergy) and replace it with plain wording.

texte: An idiom is a chunk whose meaning cannot be worked out from its words: “learn the ropes” is not about ropes but about learning how a job is done. Many idioms come from sailing (learn the ropes, on board), sport (ballpark, touch base, the ball is in your court) or accounting (the bottom line, in the red).

The form is fixed: we say “on the same page”, never “in the same page”, and “pull your weight”, never “pull your weights”. What can change is the tense of the verb (we touched base, I'll touch base) and the possessive, which agrees with the subject (she pulls her weight, they pull their weight).
At C1 the challenge is not to know many idioms but to use a few, accurately. One or two well-chosen idioms sound natural; a stream of them sounds rehearsed or even comic.
exemples: I'm still learning the ropes, so bear with me.
“Bear with me” = please be patient with me.
She really pulls her weight on this team.
She does her fair share of the work; the possessive agrees with “she”.
We touched base last week, but nothing's been decided.
The verb changes tense; the rest of the idiom stays the same.

texte: These are the idioms you will hear most often. They organise the discussion: starting, updating, postponing and informing.

lignes: touch base (with sb)
make brief contact, have a quick update
Let's touch base on Friday.
be on the same page
agree, share the same understanding
Before we start, are we all on the same page?
get the ball rolling
start something
Who wants to get the ball rolling?
keep sb in the loop
keep sb informed
Please keep me in the loop.
keep sb posted
tell sb about new developments
I'll keep you posted on the budget.
run sth by sb
ask sb for their opinion on sth
Can I run an idea by you?
take it offline
discuss it separately, outside the meeting
This is getting detailed, let's take it offline.
put a pin in it
set it aside to return to later (informal, mainly US)
Good point, let's put a pin in it for now.
the ball is in your court
it's your turn to act or decide
We've sent our offer: the ball is in their court.

sections.note: “Keep me in the loop” and “keep me posted” are near synonyms; “keep me updated” is the neutral version that works everywhere.

texte: These idioms describe how a project is going and how people work. Several are critical: “cut corners” (do something badly to save time or money) and “drop the ball” (fail to do something you were responsible for) are used to criticise, so handle them with tact.

lignes: hit the ground running
be effective from the very start
We need someone who can hit the ground running.
bring sb up to speed
give sb the latest information
Can you bring Léa up to speed on the client?
back to the drawing board
we must start again from the beginning
The client rejected it, so it's back to the drawing board.
put sth on the back burner
make sth a lower priority for now
The app redesign is on the back burner.
cut corners
do sth less well to save time or money
We can't cut corners on safety.
drop the ball
make a mistake by forgetting a task
I dropped the ball on that invoice, sorry.
go the extra mile
make more effort than expected
Our support team always goes the extra mile.
be snowed under (BrE) / swamped
have too much work
I'm snowed under this week.
call it a day
stop working for today
It's seven o'clock, let's call it a day.

exemples: I'm afraid I dropped the ball on the shipping dates.
Admitting a mistake with an idiom: direct but not dramatic.
We've put the merger on the back burner until the audit is finished.
“On the back burner” = postponed, not abandoned.

texte: Idioms about figures and results are very common in spoken reports and presentations. “The bottom line” was originally the last line of a profit and loss account (the profit or loss); by extension it means the most important fact in a situation.

lignes: a ballpark figure
a rough estimate
Can you give me a ballpark figure?
the bottom line
the key point; the final financial result
The bottom line is that we're over budget.
in the red / in the black
losing money / making a profit
The branch has been in the red for two years.
break even
make neither a profit nor a loss
We expect to break even next year.
low-hanging fruit
easy, quick gains
Let's start with the low-hanging fruit.
a win-win (situation)
a situation good for everyone
Flexible hours are a win-win.
cut your losses
stop something failing to avoid losing more
The project isn't working; it's time to cut our losses.
a game changer
something that changes a situation completely
Automation has been a game changer for us.

exemples: Ballpark, we're looking at around fifty thousand euros.
“Ballpark” alone at the start of a sentence = roughly; very spoken.
The bottom line is that we can't afford a second office.
Used to close a discussion by stating the key point.

sections.titre: Register: when to use (or avoid) an idiom
texte: In meetings, internal emails and conversations with colleagues, idioms are natural. In an official letter, a report, a contract or a first email to a client, choose the neutral equivalent.

Some idioms have become corporate jargon that many native speakers find empty: “circle back”, “move the needle”, “leverage synergies”, “think outside the box”. You must understand them, but using them constantly makes you sound like a press release.
British vs American: “snowed under” is mainly British, “swamped” is used everywhere; “put a pin in it” and “touch base” are American in origin but now common in the UK.

lignes: Let's touch base next week.
Shall we arrange a short follow-up meeting next week?
Can you give me a ballpark figure?
Could you provide an approximate estimate?
Keep me in the loop.
Please keep me informed.
We're snowed under.
We are currently dealing with a very high workload.
It's back to the drawing board.
We will need to revise the proposal entirely.
Let's circle back to this.
Let's return to this point later.

exemples: Could you provide an approximate estimate by Friday?
The formal version of “a ballpark figure”, for a client.

formule: Idiom = fixed chunk (preposition, article and noun do not change) + verb in the right tense and matching possessive; for speech and internal writing
prononciation: Stress falls on the most important content word, often the last one: on the same PAGE, back to the DRAWing board, the bottom LINE.
“ballpark” is /ˈbɔːlpɑːk/ (BrE), stressed on the first syllable; “ropes” is /rəʊps/, with a diphthong.
Grammar words are reduced: “to the” /tə ðə/ in “back to the drawing board”, “in the” /ɪn ðə/ in “in the loop”.
“touch base”: link /tʌtʃ beɪs/ with no pause; “base” rhymes with “face”.
“posted” in “keep you posted” is /ˈpəʊstɪd/: two syllables, because -ed is /ɪd/ after t.
erreurs: We are in the same page.
We're on the same page.
The preposition is part of the idiom: “on” the same page.
I'll keep you in the course.
I'll keep you posted. / I'll keep you in the loop.
A translation of the French “au courant”; the English idiom is “keep sb posted / in the loop”.
I'm overbooked this week.
I'm snowed under / swamped this week.
“Overbooked” describes a flight or hotel, not a busy person.
He doesn't pull his weights.
He doesn't pull his weight.
“Weight” stays singular in this idiom.
Let's put it in the back burner.
Let's put it on the back burner.
You put a pan “on” the back burner of a cooker.
I'm still learning the strings.
I'm still learning the ropes.
“The ropes” = how a job works; “pull strings” means using your contacts.
Let's do a brainstorming.
Let's brainstorm. / Let's have a brainstorming session.
“Brainstorm” is a verb; “a brainstorming” on its own is not standard English.
Dear Mr Lee, please give us a ballpark figure ASAP.
Dear Mr Lee, could you provide an approximate estimate at your earliest convenience?
Idioms and ASAP are too informal for a first formal email to a client.

dialogue.contexte: A Monday morning team video call between Montreal and Brussels.
lignes: Nadia
Morning, everyone. Let's get the ball rolling. Tom, can you bring us up to speed on the Lyon project?
Two idioms to open a meeting: start, and give us an update.
Tom
Sure. The bottom line is that the client didn't like the prototype, so it's back to the drawing board.
Key point first, then: we must start again.
Nadia
Oh dear. Do we have a ballpark figure for the extra cost?
She asks for a rough estimate.
Tom
Ballpark, around twelve thousand euros. But we can't cut corners on testing.
“Ballpark” alone = roughly; “cut corners” = reduce quality.
Awa
Agreed. And honestly, I'm snowed under with the Douala launch, so I can't take on much more.
She explains her heavy workload.
Nadia
Understood. Let's put the website update on the back burner, then.
A lower priority for now.
Tom
The pricing question is getting quite detailed. Shall we take it offline?
A polite way to move a detailed topic out of the meeting.
Nadia
Good idea. Tom and Awa, touch base this afternoon and keep me in the loop.
Two idioms to close: talk briefly, and keep me informed.

mots: touch base
Let's touch base after the client call.
make brief contact to share news
ballpark
We need a ballpark figure by Monday.
approximate; a rough estimate
learn the ropes
New staff spend a month learning the ropes.
learn how to do a job
bottom line
The bottom line is that sales are down.
the most important fact; the final profit or loss
back burner
The training plan is on the back burner.
low priority, waiting for later
cut corners
Never cut corners on data security.
do something badly to save time or money
drop the ball
Someone dropped the ball on the booking.
make a mistake by forgetting a task
snowed under
The accounts team is snowed under.
having too much work
break even
The shop should break even in its second year.
make neither a profit nor a loss
win-win
The new schedule is a win-win for staff and clients.
good for everyone involved

items: Can you give us a ballpark figure?

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: She really pulls her weights.

items: It's 7 p.m., let's stop working for today.

exercices.consigne: Write a short internal message (4–5 sentences) to your team about a project that is behind schedule. Use three idioms from the lesson correctly.
items: Example answer

Hi all, quick update on the Kribi project. The bottom line is that we're two weeks behind schedule, mainly because the supplier dropped the ball on the delivery. I've put the marketing plan on the back burner so we can focus on the build. Let's touch base on Thursday, and please keep me in the loop if anything changes.

a_retenir: An idiom is a fixed chunk: preposition, article and noun do not change (on the same page, pull your weight); only the tense and the possessive adapt.
Meetings and internal emails: idioms are welcome. Formal letters, reports, first contact with a client: use the neutral equivalent.
Few but accurate: one or two idioms per exchange are enough; jargon (circle back, synergy) is for understanding more than imitating.
Common traps: keep sb posted (not “in the course”), snowed under / swamped (not “overbooked”), learn the ropes (not “the strings”).
